evidence.readmeExcerpt: # rdsh-no-feedback Turn the DSH message-feedback surface off, bundled with [rdsh](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh). ## What it disables DSH ships the feedback feature as three entries in the Web profile's loader tree. This bundle carries one patch layer that sets `disabled: true` on all three: | Loader entry | Package | What it provides | | --- | --- | --- | | `message-feedback` | `@deepseek-ai/dsh-message-feedback` | the server-side `messageFeedback` Remote: per-message ratings and notes | | `ui-message-feedback` | `@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-message-feedback` | Like/Dislike in the assistant-message action strip, the dialog behind Dislike and `/feedback`, and the acknowledgement toast | | `command-feedback` | `@deepseek-ai/dsh-command-feedback` | the log-only `sessionFeedback` Remote and the human-facing `/feedback` slash command | ### Why all three, not just the UI The browser plugin declares `remote.messageFeedback` and `remote.sessionFeedback` as **required** injects, and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-message-feedback` is the only package that registers the first of those namespaces. Disabling the server half on its own would therefore leave the client plugin unable to load rather than cleanly hiding the buttons, and disabling the browser half on its own leaves a live `/feedback` command and two served Remotes with no reader. The three rows are a set. Disabling an entry does not remove it from the composed tree: the row keeps its `name` and `config` and gains `disabled: true`, which the loader honors. ### Why the sidebar row needed a client half `@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-settings-account` builds the signed-out sidebar menu from a fixed list — Settings, Feedback, Sign in — inside the component. Disabling the three packages above removes the Remote, the dialog and `/feedback`, but not that launcher row, which then opens a form this profile cannot serve. No slot or config removes it, so `client.js` hides it in the signed-out menu the component marks with its module-scoped `signedOutMenu` class, matching the label and the paper-plane glyph together so another bundle's row is never touched. A signed-in menu is left alone. Existing messages, the action strip's other buttons and every other Remote are untouched. ## Install The bundle is attached only when the feature switch is off, on every profile: ```sh rdsh features off feedback PROFILE=web ./plugins/install.sh # or: rdsh plugins install --profile web ``` Then restart DSH. The switch is a normal `rdsh.json` setting, so `rdsh settings set features.feedback false` and `rdsh features on feedback` work too. With the switch on (the default) the bundle is not attached and the stock DSH surface stays exactly as shipped. For one profile by hand: ```sh dsh plugin --profile web add "$(pwd)/plugins/rdsh-no-feedback" dsh plugin --profile web remove rdsh-no-feedback # revert ``` ## Verification - `node --test tests/no-feedback.test.mjs` parses this bundle's patch, asserts the three ids and the package each row names, and — when a `dsh` CLI and a `web` profile are present — composes the real tree with `dsh --profile web --patch .../cordis.patch.yml --dump-config` and checks that each entry came out `disabled: true`. It also runs `plugins/install.sh` against a hermetic `$DSH_HOME` to prove the bundle is attached for `features.feedback=false` on web, headless and desktop, and not otherwise. - `node --test tests/plugin-catalog.test.mjs` keeps the catalog entry, this bundle's directory and the installer's conditional in agreement. ## Caveats - The ids and package names are upstream DSH API. A rename makes the patch rows match nothing, which the loader reports as a skipped patch and then boots with the feedback surface still on (fail open). The test above composes against the installed profile, so a rename shows up there; re-check the three packages after a DSH upgrade. - The patch is applied by the profile's bundle layer, so it needs the package attached. Editing a profile's own `cordis.patch.yml` by hand is an alternative, but it is not what this bundle does. - Only the Web profile ships the browser half. On `headless` the same patch disables the server Remote and the slash command, which are present there too. # rdsh — a fast, safe Rust launcher for `dsh` [![ci](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![dashboard](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/actions/workflows/dashboard.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/actions/workflows/dashboard.yml) [![docs](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/actions/workflows/docs.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/actions/workflows/docs.yml) [![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh) [![release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh.svg)](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/releases) [![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/rdsh.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/rdsh) [![license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green.svg)](LICENSE) [![rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/rust-1.85%2B-orange.svg)](https://www.rust-lang.org/) [日本語](README.ja.md) · [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md) An independent community project; not an official DeepSeek or DeepSeek Harness project. `rdsh` is a fast, safe launcher for [DeepSeek Harness (`dsh`)](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness). It ports frequently used CLI operations (token calculation, code search, session management) to native Rust, while delegating conversation workflows and model execution transparently to upstream `dsh`. All existing arguments and options continue to work as-is. ## For AI agents Paste this before you ask an agent to work on this repository. ```text You are working on rdsh, a Rust launcher for dsh (DeepSeek Harness). - Native subcommands run in Rust. Every other argument is passed to upstream dsh unchanged. - A booted profile still runs Node.js, so conversations start and cost memory like upstream. Do not claim rdsh makes them faster or lighter. - Read AGENTS.md before editing. Do not touch credentials, published release assets or published tags. - Verify with: cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy -- -D warnings, cargo test. - Report only commands you actually ran, with their exit codes. ``` ## Why rdsh? - ⚡ **Sub-millisecond process launch**: `rdsh --version` starts in ~0.90 ms with ~2.9 MB peak RSS, versus ~88 ms and ~66 MB for Node.js-based `dsh --version`. This is process launch only: a booted agent profile still runs upstream Node.js, so conversation startup and session memory match upstream. See [Benchmarks](#benchmarks). - 🔄 **100% Drop-in Compatible**: Subcommands that are not rdsh-native are passed straight to upstream `dsh`. Existing scripts and workflows keep running unchanged. - 🛠 **Fast Native Utilities**: Estimate tokens, search code, list sessions, and run health diagnostics (`rdsh doctor`) instantly without starting Node.js. - 🛡 **Safe by Default**: Read-only commands never modify source files, credentials are never automatically synced or exported, and `rdsh_inspect` can be confined to explicitly shared files on Linux. - 🛠 **Fast Native Utilities**: Estimate tokens, search code, list sessions, and inspect local prerequisites (`rdsh doctor --json`) without starting Node.js. - 🛡 **Safe by Default**: Read-only commands never modify source files, credentials are never automatically synced or exported, and agent tools can be confined to explicitly shared files on Linux. The design rationale behind this hybrid split is documented in [docs/PHILOSOPHY.md](docs/PHILOSOPHY.md). ## Table of Contents - [Quick Start](#quick-start) - [Requirements](#requirements) - [Installation](#installation) - [Usage](#usage) - [Running with `dsh` Compatibility](#running-with-dsh-compatibility) - [Fast Native Commands](#fast-native-commands) - [Credential sharing with rdsh auth](#credential-sharing-with-rdsh-auth) - [Agent Tool Isolation](#agent-tool-isolation) - [Hook Guard](#hook-guard-rdsh-guard) - [Context Injection](#context-injection-rdsh-context) - [Dependency Graph and Change Impact](#dependency-graph-and-change-impact-rdsh-deps) - [Web UI & Dashboard](#web-ui--dashboard) - [Using with Smart-DSH](#using-with-smart-dsh) - [Benchmarks](#benchmarks) - [Safety Design](#safety-design) - [FAQ](#faq) - [Documentation](#documentation) - [Community](#community) - [Credits](#credits) - [License](#license) ## Quick Start Already using **Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code Copilot, OpenCode or Gemini CLI**? [Connect the project dashboard through MCP](docs/MCP-CLIENTS.md) to share tasks, questions and structured UI while keeping your current coding agent. This entry point requires Node.js 22+; DSH and Rust are optional. ### 1. Install (Prebuilt Binary) **Linux / macOS / WSL**: ```sh curl -fsSL https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash -s -- --from-release ``` **Windows (PowerShell)**: ```powershell $f = Join-Path $env:TEMP 'rdsh-install.ps1' Invoke-WebRequest -Uri https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 -OutFile $f -UseBasicParsing & $f -FromRelease ``` Or install the crate from crates.io (needs Rust 1.85+): ```sh cargo install rdsh ``` `cargo install` builds from source and installs the same binary as the release archives. Debian/Ubuntu and Fedora/RHEL users can also install the release [`.deb`/`.rpm`](#native-packages-deb--rpm) with `apt`/`dnf`. ### 2. Verify & Setup ```sh rdsh --version && rdsh doctor # verify install and original dsh rdsh setup # interactive setup (or rdsh setup --web for browser UI) ``` *Note: If you have an existing login from Codex CLI (ChatGPT OAuth) or opencode, import it with `rdsh auth --import --provider openai-codex`.* ### 3. Start a Conversation ```sh rdsh tui # start with TUI profile # or rdsh --profile web # start with Web profile ``` ## Requirements | Item | Detail | | --- | --- | | OS | Linux, macOS, WSL, Windows (native) | | DSH runtime | Required for conversations and agent runs (native tools and diagnostics run standalone) | | Rust | 1.85+ (only needed when building from source; prebuilt binaries require no Rust) | | Optional | Node.js 22+ for the [Node.js dashboard](dashboard/README.md); SearXNG or an Ollama API key for `search-web` | ## Installation ### Native Packages (`.deb` / `.rpm`) Linux x86_64 users on Debian/Ubuntu (and WSL) or Fedora/RHEL can install the same release binary with the OS package manager. Download the `.deb` or `.rpm` from the [latest release](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/releases/latest) and install that file directly; no extra repository is configured. ```sh sudo apt install ./rdsh__amd64.deb # Debian, Ubuntu, WSL sudo dnf install ./rdsh--1.x86_64.rpm # Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, AlmaLinux ``` `` is the release tag without its leading `v` (`0.6.0` for `v0.6.0`). The package installs `/usr/bin/rdsh` together with the licence and README, so `rdsh --version` works right after installation: no Rust toolchain, no `install.sh`. Like `rdsh-linux-x64.tar.gz`, both packages carry the glibc build, so the musl archive and `install.sh` stay the fallback for older distributions. ### Building from Source & Advanced Options **Linux / macOS / WSL**: ```sh git clone https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh.git cd rustdsh ./install.sh # build + install to ~/.local/bin/rdsh ./install.sh --as-dsh # also replace `dsh` command (original backed up as dsh-orig) ./install.sh --restore # undo the replacement ./install.sh --prefix=DIR # custom install directory (default: ~/.local/bin) ``` **Windows (PowerShell)**: ```powershell git clone https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh.git cd rustdsh .\install.ps1 # build + install to %LOCALAPPDATA%\rdsh\bin .\install.ps1 -AsDsh # also replace `dsh` command .\install.ps1 -Restore # undo the replacement .\install.ps1 -Wsl # also install inside WSL via install.sh ``` | OS | Script | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Linux / macOS | `./install.sh` | Needs `cargo` or `curl` (guided via rustup if missing). | | WSL | `./install.sh` inside distro | Auto-detects WSL. `install.ps1 -Wsl` installs in both environments. | | Windows (native) | `.\install.ps1` | Needs Rust and MSVC build tools (`winget install Rustlang.Rustup`). | ### Package Managers (Homebrew / Scoop / winget) Advanced users on macOS and Windows can let a package manager own the installed `rdsh` binary. The manifests in [packaging/](packaging/README.md) pin the exact release archives and their SHA-256 values; [docs/PACKAGE-MANAGERS.md](docs/PACKAGE-MANAGERS.md) lists the install commands and the update procedure. **macOS (Homebrew)** — installs the Apple Silicon or Intel archive: ```sh brew install --formula ./packaging/homebrew/rdsh.rb ``` **Windows (Scoop)**: ```powershell scoop install https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/main/packaging/scoop/rdsh.json ``` **Windows (winget)** — winget 1.6 or newer reads the three manifests directly; submitting them to `microsoft/winget-pkgs` stays a manual step: ```powershell winget install --manifest .\packaging\winget ``` These channels track one release at a time, so a new tag is not served until `python3 scripts/update-packaging-manifests.py --version vX.Y.Z` refreshes them. ## Usage ### Running with `dsh` Compatibility Run any standard `dsh` command unchanged: ```sh rdsh tui # equivalent to: dsh --profile tui rdsh --profile web --patch x.yml # launch with configuration overlay rdsh --dry-run tui -- --resume id # print what would be executed ``` When installed with `./install.sh --as-dsh`, typing `dsh` automatically uses the fast `rdsh` launcher. ### Fast Native Commands Native tools execute in Rust without starting Node.js: ```sh rdsh tokens ./README.md # estimate token count (~4 chars = 1 tok, CJK = 1 tok each) echo "..." | rdsh prune --max-tokens 4000 # prune context within a token budget rdsh search TODO --dir . --max 100 # fast parallel text search rdsh sessions --limit 20 --tokens # list sessions and unpacked token estimates rdsh compact ./s.jsonl # compact session JSONL (source remains untouched) rdsh doctor # check health of dsh, environment, and paths rdsh doctor --json # read-only metadata for scripts; no DSH/Node launch rdsh profiles / rdsh skills # list available profiles and skills rdsh desktop status # detect the DeepSeek Harness Desktop app and profile rdsh plugins status # essential plugins a profile is still missing rdsh plugins install --profile web # attach them after an upgrade rdsh bench --n 5 # benchmark startup speed between rdsh and dsh ``` On Windows, compressed session histories are not opened until rdsh can reject parent junctions safely; `sessions --tokens` may omit those histories and its totals are inexact. ### Plugin provisioning (`rdsh plugins`) The essential plugin tier (the upstream tools absent from `dsh-base` plus the bundled rdsh plugins) only lived in `plugins/install.sh`, and nothing runs that script by itself: upgrading the binary leaves the profile manifest untouched, so an install can miss every essential package without any signal. The same catalog is compiled into the binary, so a release install can see and close the gap without the checkout: ```sh rdsh plugins status # read-only state per package, plus the fix rdsh plugins status --profile web --json # schema 1 for scripts and dashboards rdsh plugins install # attach what the profile is missing rdsh plugins install --profile web # web/desktop defaults also add the starter set rdsh plugins install --recommended=none # the essential tier only rdsh plugins install --no-bundled # no checkout: the upstream tools only rdsh plugins install --plugins-dir # or export RDSH_PLUGINS_DIR ``` Packages go through `dsh plugin --profile add ` (`RDSH_DSH_BIN` overrides the CLI), exactly as the checkout installer does. Bundled plugins are resolved from the checkout, and an absent checkout is reported instead of being skipped quietly. `rdsh doctor` prints the same gap for every initialized profile, and `--profile desktop` forwards to `rdsh desktop install`. See [plugins/recommended.md](plugins/recommended.md) for the tiers and the ids. ### Credential sharing with rdsh auth External credentials are inventoried without showing their values. Nothing is copied until you select a source and credential. OAuth copies use DSH's existing version-1 store at $DSH_HOME/.credentials.yaml; API keys use its named refs. The selection policy contains only identifiers at $DSH_HOME/rdsh-auth-sharing.json. ```sh rdsh auth # sources, destinations, selection and undo steps rdsh auth --json # secret-free machine-readable inventory rdsh --dry-run auth --select codex:openai-codex --import # preview; writes no files rdsh auth --select codex:openai-codex --import # share only Codex OAuth rdsh auth --select opencode:openai-codex --import # OpenCode openai maps to openai-codex rdsh auth --select codex:OPENAI_API_KEY --import # separate opt-in for Codex's API key rdsh auth --select env:DEEPSEEK_API_KEY --import # explicitly persist this environment key rdsh auth --unselect codex:openai-codex # stop future copies; retain the existing copy rdsh setup # sync selected credentials, then guide setup rdsh setup --web # inventory, selection commands and explicit key save ``` For a one-time import, use `rdsh auth --import --provider openai-codex --source codex` or `rdsh auth --import --ref OPENAI_API_KEY --source codex`. These filters do not save or extend future-copy consent; `--select`/`--unselect` are separate persistent policy changes. Repeat --select/--unselect for individual credentials. Selecting enables future imports from that CLI/provider, including boot, dump-config, plugin, raw dsh delegation and setup. --import immediately applies the selection. Even a newer grant in another, unselected CLI cannot be chosen. Newer DSH grants and existing API-key refs/records remain in place. Other entries, comments and line endings are preserved. Unix credential and policy files use mode 0600. The inventory checks Codex's ~/.codex/auth.json and OpenCode's $XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode/auth.json (or its platform default data directory), plus the legacy ~/.config/opencode/auth.json fallback. Selectors for OpenCode use DSH provider IDs; opencode:openai-codex is the selector for its openai login. Environment-key persistence supports DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. These are format/presence checks, not live authentication tests. An environment variable already supplied to rdsh is inherited by DSH and its child processes without rdsh writing a file. The JSON inventory marks this route persistent=false, lists its destination and explains how to stop/revoke it. Using the reference does not opt in to storing it. setup --yes no longer saves every environment key; choose each one with auth --select env:NAME --import. Interactive setup and the web form still allow an explicit, individual key save. **Scope and undo:** saved entries are available to every DSH profile using the same DSH_HOME. Unselect stops future rdsh imports; it does not delete a saved copy or invalidate a running process. Stop DSH and remove the named record/ref from the credential store to stop using a saved copy. To invalidate the credential itself, revoke the OAuth grant or rotate the API key at its provider. That may also disconnect the source CLI. This controls rdsh copying, not DSH's own refreshes, inherited environment access or an OS sandbox. **Migration:** existing DSH credentials are retained. A missing policy selects nothing, including for legacy auth --import. RDSH_AUTH_AUTOSYNC=1 does not restore the old import-all behavior. Inventory and preview first, then choose the sources you need. RDSH_AUTH_AUTOSYNC=0 disables automatic imports while keeping the selection; an explicit auth --import still works. Invalid/unreadable policies fail closed instead of falling back to legacy sync. Consent changes and rdsh credential writes share a lock, so a completed unselect cannot be bypassed by a queued rdsh import using an earlier policy. After a crashed writer, check that no rdsh auth/setup writer is active before removing $DSH_HOME/.rdsh-auth-sharing.lock; the launcher skips copying while it is locked. setup --web issues a new local access key at startup in its #key=... URL. The tab retains that key; status reads, key saves and closing require it. Keep the startup URL private. The page shows copy destinations and separate unselect, saved-copy removal and provider revocation steps before a key save. ### Optional extras (off by default) Server-type features and the privacy-sensitive switches (`discord`, `telemetry`) stay off until enabled, so a plain install remains a fast, telemetry-free dsh: ```sh rdsh settings set extras.enable serve,search-web rdsh settings get extras.enable ``` | Extra | Command | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | `serve` | `rdsh serve` (default :38080) | Local status page, localhost only, per-launch key. | | `search-web` | `rdsh search-web "query" --limit 5` | SearXNG by default; `--provider ollama` uses `OLLAMA_API_KEY`; `--auto-start` starts the bundled local SearXNG compose service. See [Web search](docs/WEB-SEARCH.md). | To connect an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that dsh does not ship (HAI, Command Code, Sarashina, a home llama.cpp / vLLM / LM Studio / Ollama server), add it as a profile route: ```sh rdsh provider add hai --model deepseek-v4-flash # key from HAI_API_KEY or --key-stdin rdsh provider add commandcode --model deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash # key from COMMANDCODE_API_KEY rdsh provider add sarashina # key from SARASHINA_API_KEY; mini and nano built in rdsh provider add local-openai --base-url http://host:8080/v1 --discover --no-key rdsh provider list # presets, per-profile route and key status ``` Details: [docs/PROVIDERS.md](docs/PROVIDERS.md). ### Model Catalog (`rdsh models`) DeepSeek Harness answers "which models can this provider serve?" from the catalog bundled in its `@earendil-works/pi-ai` dependency, which is generated when that package is published. Anything a provider changes afterwards is absent from the picker until that dependency is upgraded — and a profile that lists `models:` explicitly replaces the bundled catalog for the route anyway. `rdsh models` reads the provider's own catalog (the local Codex CLI, or Kimi Code's `/v1/models` endpoint with the profile's API key) and folds it into the profile: ```sh rdsh models # read-only: missing ids and stale names rdsh models --provider kimi-coding # one provider only rdsh models sync # add missing entries, refresh stale names rdsh models sync --profile web --dry-run # preview one profile ``` Nothing is deleted, an existing entry keeps every other byte (a name the provider's current one already contains is left as written), and a profile the command does not recognize is refused instead of rewritten. The harness picks the changes up on the next config reload or restart. ### Agent Tool Isolation Delegated agent tools keep normal file access by default: the model reads and writes the project like any other tool. `--share-file` isolates **`rdsh_inspect` only**. On Linux (with bubblewrap and prlimit) that tool sees just the files you explicitly share: ```sh rdsh --share-file README.md --share-file src/main.rs --profile tui ``` From `rdsh_inspect`, only the shared files are mounted read-only, host files stay out of reach and the sandbox has no network. Turn the same boundary on for every run with `rdsh features on agent_tool_sandbox` (off again with `rdsh features off agent_tool_sandbox`, or force it with `RDSH_SECURITY=1`). Other DSH tools (`bash`, `read`, `write`, `run_code`, ...) are **not** isolated and follow upstream DSH permissions and approvals. Startup prints `[rdsh security] rdsh_inspect is isolated; other DSH tools use upstream permissions`. ### Hook Guard (`rdsh guard`) Integrates with DSH `hooks.json` to inspect and block dangerous commands before execution: ```sh echo "$input" | rdsh guard --deny "rm -rf /*" --deny "*token*" ``` For an opt-in structured check of supported file tools, pass a policy file. This example permits `Read` only under one existing project directory: ```json { "schema": 1, "rules": [ { "id": "project-read", "tool": "Read", "access": "read", "roots": ["/absolute/project/path"] } ] } ``` ```sh echo "$hook_json" | rdsh guard --policy-file ./hook-policy.json --json ``` The structured classifier supports the `Read`, `Write`, and `Edit` file-path schemas. It canonicalizes the working directory and target, checks the selected tool and read/write scope against existing policy roots, and reports `allow`, `deny`, or `unknown` with a non-sensitive reason. In JSON mode an `allow` is classification only and omits `decision`; the host still owns permission and approval. Unknown tools, shell commands, malformed input, and unsupported tool arguments fail closed. Shell parsing and network destinations are not implemented. Path checks are advisory and can race with later filesystem changes; this hook is not an OS sandbox. Use the actual execution sandbox for enforcement. ```json { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "rdsh guard --deny \"rm -rf /*\"" }] } ] } } ``` ### Context Injection (`rdsh context`) `rdsh context inject` assembles this turn's context — goal, constraints, decisions, working set, git state, retrieved code, and curated memory — and emits it in the DSH `UserPromptSubmit` hook contract, so the model sees it without any copy-paste: ```sh rdsh features on context_engine # the engine is opt-in rdsh context hook install # merges $DSH_HOME/hooks.json (idempotent) rdsh context hook status --json ``` The hook is fail-open: it never blocks a prompt and always exits 0. Only an unreadable settings document or an unparseable payload inject nothing at all; a corrupt index or a missed deadline drops just what depends on them — the graph or the code search — and still injects goal, constraints, and memory. Injection has its own budget (`context.inject_budget`, default 1200 tokens) and deadline (`context.inject_deadline_ms`, default 1200 ms); once the deadline passes the code search is skipped and only memory, goal, and constraints go out. Memory holds curated items, not a transcript dump: ```sh rdsh context remember "Keep the API compatible" --kind constraint rdsh context distill --session ~/.dsh/sessions///session.v4.jsonl.zstd --apply rdsh context memory --json # active and superseded entries rdsh context forget mem_ab12cd34ef56 ``` `distill` reads user turns only (zstd session logs included) and extracts decisions, constraints, and retractions with deterministic markers, superseding an older overlapping entry instead of guessing. `rdsh context build --require-stable` exits 3 unless the snapshot is provably stable: a file or git state that changed during assembly counts, and so does a git state it cannot read, so a stale or unknown snapshot is never reported as fresh. ### Dependency Graph and Change Impact (`rdsh deps`) ```sh rdsh deps build # incremental index under $DSH_HOME/rdsh-index rdsh deps query engine_score # where a symbol is defined and referenced rdsh deps impact src/context.rs # direct/transitive dependents + affected tests ``` The extractor covers Rust, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, and Go and records imports, definitions, and static call sites per file. Unchanged files (same size and mtime) are reused, so repeated runs stay fast. It is a static approximation: dynamic dispatch, indirect calls, macros, and generated code remain explicitly `unknown` and are reported as unresolved counts rather than guessed, and a missing index means "no information", never "no dependencies". When the index exists, `rdsh context build` and `rdsh context inject` also pull in the graph neighbours of the files their search matched, so a retrieved excerpt arrives with the files it actually depends on. Native execution overhead is ~1 ms per invocation. ## Low-end hosts Default profile: `RDSH_DEFAULT_PROFILE`, then `general.default_profile` in rdsh settings, then local `tui`, else a guided error. Set the saved default with `rdsh settings set general.default_profile web`; an explicit `--profile ` keeps its precedence. rdsh aims to remain useful on modest machines: older x86-64 CPUs, older Linux distributions, and hosts without Node.js installed. - **Faster Node startup.** When rdsh launches dsh, it sets `NODE_COMPILE_CACHE` to `~/.cache/rdsh-node-compile-cache`, letting Node reuse compiled code across launches (Node 22.1 or newer; older versions ignore it). An existing `NODE_COMPILE_CACHE` value is preserved. Set `RDSH_NODE_COMPILE_CACHE=0`, or use `--passthrough` / `RDSH_PASSTHROUGH=1`, to opt out. Set `RDSH_NODE_COMPILE_CACHE=` to keep the cache at a fixed location instead of the default, fo

evidence.readmeExcerpt: # Scoped PTC tool catalog This optional Cordis bundle adds tool discovery to an existing, authorized DSH PTC composition. It supports `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools@0.2.0-rc.2` and uses the public registry, original SDK renderers and `system-prompt/assemble` waterfall. The original `run_code`, runtime provider, scheduler, guards, approval policies and canonical output validation retain execution ownership. The guarded rdsh launcher forces Native tools. This bundle refuses activation there with `RDSH_CATALOG_GUARDED_NATIVE`; it does not enable PTC in that launcher. Nothing installs the bundle or changes an existing user profile automatically. MCP connection, OAuth and deferred server loading remain owned by their existing services; this catalog enumerates only registered tools. ## Configuration For an original DSH composition that already supplies `tools`, `systemPrompt` and `ptcRuntime`, add this local package through the existing DSH bundle/profile mechanism. Its [bundle patch](cordis.patch.yml) supplies these defaults: ```yaml config: inlineTokenBudget: 16384 inlineTools: [] maxSearchResults: 20 ``` `inlineTools` is an explicit ordered list of exact names whose declarations may be included after the two discovery helpers. A name outside the calling scope is never displayed. A declaration that does not fit stays discoverable. If even the mandatory discovery declarations cannot fit, prompt assembly fails with `RDSH_CATALOG_BUDGET` and an actionable size, rather than omitting the discovery API. A scope that restricts or shadows those helpers fails with `RDSH_CATALOG_SCOPE_UNAVAILABLE`. The budget counts UTF-8 bytes as a conservative token upper bound for byte-based tokenizers. It is deliberately conservative, **not measured DeepSeek token usage**. It covers the complete replacement `tools:sdk` section, including existing execution instructions and discovery guidance. Other system-prompt sections, native wire schemas in `both` mode, returned describe results, and upstream assembly allocations are outside that budget. Only the two helpers and explicit `inlineTools` influence this SDK text. Adding an unrelated tool/schema does not rewrite it. The public waterfall still runs after upstream assembles the full SDK, so this reduces model input cost without claiming to reduce upstream assembly CPU or memory. ## Discovery from the original PTC program ```ts const found = await tools.rdsh_catalog_search({ query: "failed deployment build logs", namespace: "mcp/github", limit: 3, }); if (found.status !== "ok" || found.tools.length === 0) return found; return await tools.rdsh_catalog_describe({ name: found.tools[0].name, revision: found.revision, }); ``` After reading the complete returned schema/declaration, invoke the exact name inside the original PTC program, for example `await tools[exactName](args)` in TypeScript. Python uses its original SDK and `getattr(tools, exact_name)(args)`. The returned declaration is reference text, not executable code to evaluate. - `rdsh_catalog_search` ranks names and descriptions, supports exact namespace prefix boundaries (`.`, `/`, `:`, `__`), and pages an empty query as a thin catalog. `offset`, `limit`, and `nextOffset` describe tool pagination; namespace summaries and description previews report truncation explicitly. - `identifier` filters one normalization collision group. Normalization is diagnostic only. Calls always use exact original names; no alias is created. - `rdsh_catalog_describe` returns complete input/output JSON Schemas, a schema digest and the declaration from the **original** TypeScript/Python renderer. Missing and restricted names return the same `not_found` result, without acknowledging a namespace, collision group, schema or existence. - `revision` identifies the current visible names/descriptions and detects changed search pages. A describe result's separate `schemaDigest` identifies its input/output schemas. Results are recomputed for each calling scope; there is no cross-scope cache or durable tool-state storage. Scope membership is discovery eligibility. Argument-dependent guards, approval and current execution policy can still refuse a discovered call. Search does not simulate a tool body or an approval. Restriction/permission changes after discovery remain authoritative at original nested dispatch. ## Verification and comparison From the repository checkout: ```sh npm ci --prefix plugins/rdsh-ptc-catalog --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund npm test --prefix plugins/rdsh-ptc-catalog node plugins/rdsh-ptc-catalog/benchmark.mjs --output /new/path/benchmark.json ``` The benchmark writes a new file exclusively. It compares 1,000 visible tools and 80 fixed query/execution fixtures against the original full inline SDK. It records encoded input payload size (`js-tiktoken` / `cl100k_base`), fixture lookup success, incorrect body calls, outer PTC submissions, nested dispatches, assembly time and prompt stability. The baseline knows the expected exact name. Search and describe share one discovery submission; the invocation uses a second submission. These are fixture/protocol measurements, not model quality, DeepSeek tokenizer measurements, real provider usage or billed cost. Tests also execute a fixed program through DSH's original Node provider in a fresh home/workspace without inherited provider credentials. They verify complete types, hidden-tool refusal, actual nested events and guard refusal. That execution fixture uses a full-access policy and makes no confinement claim. The separate mandatory [guarded-runtime probe](../../tests/guarded-runtime-probe.mjs) verifies that this bundle cannot lift rdsh's Native/kernel boundary. GitHub CI runs the catalog tests and benchmark on Linux, macOS and Windows, and retains the benchmark report as an artifact. Source-specific results and new/old output are in [PTC catalog evidence](../../docs/evidence/ptc-catalog/README.md). Upstream contracts: [tools API](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/blob/f97c0438fb1608bbc4c08c88a27344249795ea22/docs/tool-catalog.md), [system-prompt waterfall](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/blob/f97c0438fb1608bbc4c08c88a27344249795ea22/docs/subsystems/system-prompt.md), [PTC provider](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/blob/f97c0438fb1608bbc4c08c88a27344249795ea22/docs/subsystems/ptc-runtime.md). # rdsh — a fast, safe Rust launcher for `dsh` [![ci](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![dashboard](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/actions/workflows/dashboard.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/actions/workflows/dashboard.yml) [![docs](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/actions/workflows/docs.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/actions/workflows/docs.yml) [![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh) [![release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh.svg)](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/releases) [![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/rdsh.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/rdsh) [![license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green.svg)](LICENSE) [![rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/rust-1.85%2B-orange.svg)](https://www.rust-lang.org/) [日本語](README.ja.md) · [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md) An independent community project; not an official DeepSeek or DeepSeek Harness project. `rdsh` is a fast, safe launcher for [DeepSeek Harness (`dsh`)](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness). It ports frequently used CLI operations (token calculation, code search, session management) to native Rust, while delegating conversation workflows and model execution transparently to upstream `dsh`. All existing arguments and options continue to work as-is. ## For AI agents Paste this before you ask an agent to work on this repository. ```text You are working on rdsh, a Rust launcher for dsh (DeepSeek Harness). - Native subcommands run in Rust. Every other argument is passed to upstream dsh unchanged. - A booted profile still runs Node.js, so conversations start and cost memory like upstream. Do not claim rdsh makes them faster or lighter. - Read AGENTS.md before editing. Do not touch credentials, published release assets or published tags. - Verify with: cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy -- -D warnings, cargo test. - Report only commands you actually ran, with their exit codes. ``` ## Why rdsh? - ⚡ **Sub-millisecond process launch**: `rdsh --version` starts in ~0.90 ms with ~2.9 MB peak RSS, versus ~88 ms and ~66 MB for Node.js-based `dsh --version`. This is process launch only: a booted agent profile still runs upstream Node.js, so conversation startup and session memory match upstream. See [Benchmarks](#benchmarks). - 🔄 **100% Drop-in Compatible**: Subcommands that are not rdsh-native are passed straight to upstream `dsh`. Existing scripts and workflows keep running unchanged. - 🛠 **Fast Native Utilities**: Estimate tokens, search code, list sessions, and run health diagnostics (`rdsh doctor`) instantly without starting Node.js. - 🛡 **Safe by Default**: Read-only commands never modify source files, credentials are never automatically synced or exported, and `rdsh_inspect` can be confined to explicitly shared files on Linux. - 🛠 **Fast Native Utilities**: Estimate tokens, search code, list sessions, and inspect local prerequisites (`rdsh doctor --json`) without starting Node.js. - 🛡 **Safe by Default**: Read-only commands never modify source files, credentials are never automatically synced or exported, and agent tools can be confined to explicitly shared files on Linux. The design rationale behind this hybrid split is documented in [docs/PHILOSOPHY.md](docs/PHILOSOPHY.md). ## Table of Contents - [Quick Start](#quick-start) - [Requirements](#requirements) - [Installation](#installation) - [Usage](#usage) - [Running with `dsh` Compatibility](#running-with-dsh-compatibility) - [Fast Native Commands](#fast-native-commands) - [Credential sharing with rdsh auth](#credential-sharing-with-rdsh-auth) - [Agent Tool Isolation](#agent-tool-isolation) - [Hook Guard](#hook-guard-rdsh-guard) - [Context Injection](#context-injection-rdsh-context) - [Dependency Graph and Change Impact](#dependency-graph-and-change-impact-rdsh-deps) - [Web UI & Dashboard](#web-ui--dashboard) - [Using with Smart-DSH](#using-with-smart-dsh) - [Benchmarks](#benchmarks) - [Safety Design](#safety-design) - [FAQ](#faq) - [Documentation](#documentation) - [Community](#community) - [Credits](#credits) - [License](#license) ## Quick Start Already using **Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code Copilot, OpenCode or Gemini CLI**? [Connect the project dashboard through MCP](docs/MCP-CLIENTS.md) to share tasks, questions and structured UI while keeping your current coding agent. This entry point requires Node.js 22+; DSH and Rust are optional. ### 1. Install (Prebuilt Binary) **Linux / macOS / WSL**: ```sh curl -fsSL https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash -s -- --from-release ``` **Windows (PowerShell)**: ```powershell $f = Join-Path $env:TEMP 'rdsh-install.ps1' Invoke-WebRequest -Uri https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 -OutFile $f -UseBasicParsing & $f -FromRelease ``` Or install the crate from crates.io (needs Rust 1.85+): ```sh cargo install rdsh ``` `cargo install` builds from source and installs the same binary as the release archives. Debian/Ubuntu and Fedora/RHEL users can also install the release [`.deb`/`.rpm`](#native-packages-deb--rpm) with `apt`/`dnf`. ### 2. Verify & Setup ```sh rdsh --version && rdsh doctor # verify install and original dsh rdsh setup # interactive setup (or rdsh setup --web for browser UI) ``` *Note: If you have an existing login from Codex CLI (ChatGPT OAuth) or opencode, import it with `rdsh auth --import --provider openai-codex`.* ### 3. Start a Conversation ```sh rdsh tui # start with TUI profile # or rdsh --profile web # start with Web profile ``` ## Requirements | Item | Detail | | --- | --- | | OS | Linux, macOS, WSL, Windows (native) | | DSH runtime | Required for conversations and agent runs (native tools and diagnostics run standalone) | | Rust | 1.85+ (only needed when building from source; prebuilt binaries require no Rust) | | Optional | Node.js 22+ for the [Node.js dashboard](dashboard/README.md); SearXNG or an Ollama API key for `search-web` | ## Installation ### Native Packages (`.deb` / `.rpm`) Linux x86_64 users on Debian/Ubuntu (and WSL) or Fedora/RHEL can install the same release binary with the OS package manager. Download the `.deb` or `.rpm` from the [latest release](https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/releases/latest) and install that file directly; no extra repository is configured. ```sh sudo apt install ./rdsh__amd64.deb # Debian, Ubuntu, WSL sudo dnf install ./rdsh--1.x86_64.rpm # Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, AlmaLinux ``` `` is the release tag without its leading `v` (`0.6.0` for `v0.6.0`). The package installs `/usr/bin/rdsh` together with the licence and README, so `rdsh --version` works right after installation: no Rust toolchain, no `install.sh`. Like `rdsh-linux-x64.tar.gz`, both packages carry the glibc build, so the musl archive and `install.sh` stay the fallback for older distributions. ### Building from Source & Advanced Options **Linux / macOS / WSL**: ```sh git clone https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh.git cd rustdsh ./install.sh # build + install to ~/.local/bin/rdsh ./install.sh --as-dsh # also replace `dsh` command (original backed up as dsh-orig) ./install.sh --restore # undo the replacement ./install.sh --prefix=DIR # custom install directory (default: ~/.local/bin) ``` **Windows (PowerShell)**: ```powershell git clone https://github.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh.git cd rustdsh .\install.ps1 # build + install to %LOCALAPPDATA%\rdsh\bin .\install.ps1 -AsDsh # also replace `dsh` command .\install.ps1 -Restore # undo the replacement .\install.ps1 -Wsl # also install inside WSL via install.sh ``` | OS | Script | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Linux / macOS | `./install.sh` | Needs `cargo` or `curl` (guided via rustup if missing). | | WSL | `./install.sh` inside distro | Auto-detects WSL. `install.ps1 -Wsl` installs in both environments. | | Windows (native) | `.\install.ps1` | Needs Rust and MSVC build tools (`winget install Rustlang.Rustup`). | ### Package Managers (Homebrew / Scoop / winget) Advanced users on macOS and Windows can let a package manager own the installed `rdsh` binary. The manifests in [packaging/](packaging/README.md) pin the exact release archives and their SHA-256 values; [docs/PACKAGE-MANAGERS.md](docs/PACKAGE-MANAGERS.md) lists the install commands and the update procedure. **macOS (Homebrew)** — installs the Apple Silicon or Intel archive: ```sh brew install --formula ./packaging/homebrew/rdsh.rb ``` **Windows (Scoop)**: ```powershell scoop install https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jimoto-no-llm/rustdsh/main/packaging/scoop/rdsh.json ``` **Windows (winget)** — winget 1.6 or newer reads the three manifests directly; submitting them to `microsoft/winget-pkgs` stays a manual step: ```powershell winget install --manifest .\packaging\winget ``` These channels track one release at a time, so a new tag is not served until `python3 scripts/update-packaging-manifests.py --version vX.Y.Z` refreshes them. ## Usage ### Running with `dsh` Compatibility Run any standard `dsh` command unchanged: ```sh rdsh tui # equivalent to: dsh --profile tui rdsh --profile web --patch x.yml # launch with configuration overlay rdsh --dry-run tui -- --resume id # print what would be executed ``` When installed with `./install.sh --as-dsh`, typing `dsh` automatically uses the fast `rdsh` launcher. ### Fast Native Commands Native tools execute in Rust without starting Node.js: ```sh rdsh tokens ./README.md # estimate token count (~4 chars = 1 tok, CJK = 1 tok each) echo "..." | rdsh prune --max-tokens 4000 # prune context within a token budget rdsh search TODO --dir . --max 100 # fast parallel text search rdsh sessions --limit 20 --tokens # list sessions and unpacked token estimates rdsh compact ./s.jsonl # compact session JSONL (source remains untouched) rdsh doctor # check health of dsh, environment, and paths rdsh doctor --json # read-only metadata for scripts; no DSH/Node launch rdsh profiles / rdsh skills # list available profiles and skills rdsh desktop status # detect the DeepSeek Harness Desktop app and profile rdsh plugins status # essential plugins a profile is still missing rdsh plugins install --profile web # attach them after an upgrade rdsh bench --n 5 # benchmark startup speed between rdsh and dsh ``` On Windows, compressed session histories are not opened until rdsh can reject parent junctions safely; `sessions --tokens` may omit those histories and its totals are inexact. ### Plugin provisioning (`rdsh plugins`) The essential plugin tier (the upstream tools absent from `dsh-base` plus the bundled rdsh plugins) only lived in `plugins/install.sh`, and nothing runs that script by itself: upgrading the binary leaves the profile manifest untouched, so an install can miss every essential package without any signal. The same catalog is compiled into the binary, so a release install can see and close the gap without the checkout: ```sh rdsh plugins status # read-only state per package, plus the fix rdsh plugins status --profile web --json # schema 1 for scripts and dashboards rdsh plugins install # attach what the profile is missing rdsh plugins install --profile web # web/desktop defaults also add the starter set rdsh plugins install --recommended=none # the essential tier only rdsh plugins install --no-bundled # no checkout: the upstream tools only rdsh plugins install --plugins-dir # or export RDSH_PLUGINS_DIR ``` Packages go through `dsh plugin --profile add ` (`RDSH_DSH_BIN` overrides the CLI), exactly as the checkout installer does. Bundled plugins are resolved from the checkout, and an absent checkout is reported instead of being skipped quietly. `rdsh doctor` prints the same gap for every initialized profile, and `--profile desktop` forwards to `rdsh desktop install`. See [plugins/recommended.md](plugins/recommended.md) for the tiers and the ids. ### Credential sharing with rdsh auth External credentials are inventoried without showing their values. Nothing is copied until you select a source and credential. OAuth copies use DSH's existing version-1 store at $DSH_HOME/.credentials.yaml; API keys use its named refs. The selection policy contains only identifiers at $DSH_HOME/rdsh-auth-sharing.json. ```sh rdsh auth # sources, destinations, selection and undo steps rdsh auth --json # secret-free machine-readable inventory rdsh --dry-run auth --select codex:openai-codex --import # preview; writes no files rdsh auth --select codex:openai-codex --import # share only Codex OAuth rdsh auth --select opencode:openai-codex --import # OpenCode openai maps to openai-codex rdsh auth --select codex:OPENAI_API_KEY --import # separate opt-in for Codex's API key rdsh auth --select env:DEEPSEEK_API_KEY --import # explicitly persist this environment key rdsh auth --unselect codex:openai-codex # stop future copies; retain the existing copy rdsh setup # sync selected credentials, then guide setup rdsh setup --web # inventory, selection commands and explicit key save ``` For a one-time import, use `rdsh auth --import --provider openai-codex --source codex` or `rdsh auth --import --ref OPENAI_API_KEY --source codex`. These filters do not save or extend future-copy consent; `--select`/`--unselect` are separate persistent policy changes. Repeat --select/--unselect for individual credentials. Selecting enables future imports from that CLI/provider, including boot, dump-config, plugin, raw dsh delegation and setup. --import immediately applies the selection. Even a newer grant in another, unselected CLI cannot be chosen. Newer DSH grants and existing API-key refs/records remain in place. Other entries, comments and line endings are preserved. Unix credential and policy files use mode 0600. The inventory checks Codex's ~/.codex/auth.json and OpenCode's $XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode/auth.json (or its platform default data directory), plus the legacy ~/.config/opencode/auth.json fallback. Selectors for OpenCode use DSH provider IDs; opencode:openai-codex is the selector for its openai login. Environment-key persistence supports DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. These are format/presence checks, not live authentication tests. An environment variable already supplied to rdsh is inherited by DSH and its child processes without rdsh writing a file. The JSON inventory marks this route persistent=false, lists its destination and explains how to stop/revoke it. Using the reference does not opt in to storing it. setup --yes no longer saves every environment key; choose each one with auth --select env:NAME --import. Interactive setup and the web form still allow an explicit, individual key save. **Scope and undo:** saved entries are available to every DSH profile using the same DSH_HOME. Unselect stops future rdsh imports; it does not delete a saved copy or invalidate a running process. Stop DSH and remove the named record/ref from the credential store to stop using a saved copy. To invalidate the credential itself, revoke the OAuth grant or rotate the API key at its provider. That may also disconnect the source CLI. This controls rdsh copying, not DSH's own refreshes, inherited environment access or an OS sandbox. **Migration:** existing DSH credentials are retained. A missing policy selects nothing, including for legacy auth --import. RDSH_AUTH_AUTOSYNC=1 does not restore the old import-all behavior. Inventory and preview first, then choose the sources you need. RDSH_AUTH_AUTOSYNC=0 disables automatic imports while keeping the selection; an explicit auth --import still works. Invalid/unreadable policies fail closed instead of falling back to legacy sync. Consent changes and rdsh credential writes share a lock, so a completed unselect cannot be bypassed by a queued rdsh import using an earlier policy. After a crashed writer, check that no rdsh auth/setup writer is active before removing $DSH_HOME/.rdsh-auth-sharing.lock; the launcher skips copying while it is locked. setup --web issues a new local access key at startup in its #key=... URL. The tab retains that key; status reads, key saves and closing require it. Keep the startup URL private. The page shows copy destinations and separate unselect, saved-copy removal and provider revocation steps before a key save. ### Optional extras (off by default) Server-type features and the privacy-sensitive switches (`discord`, `telemetry`) stay off until enabled, so a plain install remains a fast, telemetry-free dsh: ```sh rdsh settings set extras.enable serve,search-web rdsh settings get extras.enable ``` | Extra | Command | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | `serve` | `rdsh serve` (default :38080) | Local status page, localhost only, per-launch key. | | `search-web` | `rdsh search-web "query" --limit 5` | SearXNG by default; `--provider ollama` uses `OLLAMA_API_KEY`; `--auto-start` starts the bundled local SearXNG compose service. See [Web search](docs/WEB-SEARCH.md). | To connect an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that dsh does not ship (HAI, Command Code, Sarashina, a home llama.cpp / vLLM / LM Studio / Ollama server), add it as a profile route: ```sh rdsh provider add hai --model deepseek-v4-flash # key from HAI_API_KEY or --key-stdin rdsh provider add commandcode --model deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash # key from COMMANDCODE_API_KEY rdsh provider add sarashina # key from SARASHINA_API_KEY; mini and nano built in rdsh provider add local-openai --base-url http://host:8080/v1 --discover --no-key rdsh provider list # presets, per-profile route and key status ``` Details: [docs/PROVIDERS.md](docs/PROVIDERS.md). ### Model Catalog (`rdsh models`) DeepSeek Harness answers "which models can this provider serve?" from the catalog bundled in its `@earendil-works/pi-ai` dependency, which is generated when that package is published. Anything a provider changes afterwards is absent from the picker until that dependency is upgraded — and a profile that lists `models:` explicitly replaces the bundled catalog for the route anyway. `rdsh models` reads the provider's own catalog (the local Codex CLI, or Kimi Code's `/v1/models` endpoint with the profile's API key) and folds it into the profile: ```sh rdsh models # read-only: missing ids and stale names rdsh models --provider kimi-coding # one provider only rdsh models sync # add missing entries, refresh stale names rdsh models sync --profile web --dry-run # preview one profile ``` Nothing is deleted, an existing entry keeps every other byte (a name the provider's current one already contains is left as written), and a profile the command does not recognize is refused instead of rewritten. The harness picks the changes up on the next config reload or restart. ### Agent Tool Isolation Delegated agent tools keep normal file access by default: the model reads and writes the project like any other tool. `--share-file` isolates **`rdsh_inspect` only**. On Linux (with bubblewrap and prlimit) that tool sees just the files you explicitly share: ```sh rdsh --share-file README.md --share-file src/main.rs --profile tui ``` From `rdsh_inspect`, only the shared files are mounted read-only, host files stay out of reach and the sandbox has no network. Turn the same boundary on for every run with `rdsh features on agent_tool_sandbox` (off again with `rdsh features off agent_tool_sandbox`, or force it with `RDSH_SECURITY=1`). Other DSH tools (`bash`, `read`, `write`, `run_code`, ...) are **not** isolated and follow upstream DSH permissions and approvals. Startup prints `[rdsh security] rdsh_inspect is isolated; other DSH tools use upstream permissions`. ### Hook Guard (`rdsh guard`) Integrates with DSH `hooks.json` to inspect and block dangerous commands before execution: ```sh echo "$input" | rdsh guard --deny "rm -rf /*" --deny "*token*" ``` For an opt-in structured check of supported file tools, pass a policy file. This example permits `Read` only under one existing project directory: ```json { "schema": 1, "rules": [ { "id": "project-read", "tool": "Read", "access": "read", "roots": ["/absolute/project/path"] } ] } ``` ```sh echo "$hook_json" | rdsh guard --policy-file ./hook-policy.json --json ``` The structured classifier supports the `Read`, `Write`, and `Edit` file-path schemas. It canonicalizes the working directory and target, checks the selected tool and read/write scope against existing policy roots, and reports `allow`, `deny`, or `unknown` with a non-sensitive reason. In JSON mode an `allow` is classification only and omits `decision`; the host still owns permission and approval. Unknown tools, shell commands, malformed input, and unsupported tool arguments fail closed. Shell parsing and network destinations are not implemented. Path checks are advisory and can race with later filesystem changes; this hook is not an OS sandbox. Use the actual execution sandbox for enforcement. ```json { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "rdsh guard --deny \"rm -rf /*\"" }] } ] } } ``` ### Context Injection (`rdsh context`) `rdsh context inject` assembles this turn's context — goal, constraints, decisions, working set, git state, retrieved code, and curated memory — and emits it in the DSH `UserPromptSubmit` hook contract, so the model sees it without any copy-paste: ```sh rdsh features on context_engine # the engine is opt-in rdsh context hook install # merges $DSH_HOME/hooks.json (idempotent) rdsh context hook status --json ``` The hook is fail-open: it never blocks a prompt and always exits 0. Only an unreadable settings document or an unparseable payload inject nothing at all; a corrupt index or a missed deadline drops just what depends on them — the graph or the code search — and still injects goal, constraints, and memory. Injection has its own budget (`context.inject_budget`, default 1200 tokens) and deadline (`context.inject_deadline_ms`, default 1200 ms); once the deadline passes the code search is skipped and only memory, goal, and constraints go out. Memory holds curated items, not a transcript dump: ```sh rdsh context remember "Keep the API compatible" --kind constraint rdsh context distill --session ~/.dsh/sessions///session.v4.jsonl.zstd --apply rdsh context memory --json # active and superseded entries rdsh context forget mem_ab12cd34ef56 ``` `distill` reads user turns only (zstd session logs included) and extracts decisions, constraints, and retractions with deterministic markers, superseding an older overlapping entry instead of guessing. `rdsh cont
